passage: When I told my group chat about the diagnosis, four friends replied within minutes. Yash didn't, and then Yash didn't for three weeks. I checked my phone more than I want to admit. It hurt, like being crossed off a list. But I remembered how stiff and awkward Yash had been at a cousin's funeral, and I wondered if this was the same. So I sent a plain message: "I'm not after wise words. A text about nothing, or a chai visit, would mean a lot." An hour later Yash replied with a bad joke about hospital food, and on Saturday turned up with samosas, standing in the doorway until I laughed. I keep the four who stayed close too. — Rashmi

qa.a: Yash stayed silent for three weeks.

qa.q: Why did Rashmi feel crossed off a list, and what made Rashmi doubt that reading?
qa.a: The silence hurt. Then Rashmi recalled Yash being stiff and awkward at a cousin's funeral, which hinted at discomfort rather than lack of care.

qa.q: What did Rashmi do that helped, and why?
qa.a: Rashmi told Yash plainly what would help, a text or a chai visit. That took away the worry about finding the right words.

qa.q: What might Yash have been feeling during the three weeks of silence?
qa.a: Probably discomfort and not knowing what to say. The joke about hospital food and the samosas suggest Yash did care.

grounding: A friend disappears after a diagnosis, likely from discomfort not lack of care; the person says how to help and keeps those who stay close.

passage:
Dear Zubin,

I've written this four times. Here's the plain version.

When I told you about the diagnosis in March, you hugged me hard and said, "Anything you need." Then you went quiet. No calls. You didn't come to the hospital. I heard from Aman you were at the match on the day of my surgery.

It hurt, more than I'll admit. At first I thought you'd stopped caring.

But I know you. You were the one who couldn't go to your grandfather's funeral because you didn't know what to do with your face. I think this is the same. You don't know what to say.

So I'll tell you. You don't have to say anything wise. Send me a stupid meme on Tuesdays. Come on Saturday and watch cricket with me, even if we just shout at the screen.

I miss you. That's all.

Lokesh

qa.q: What did Zubin say when Lokesh first shared the diagnosis?
What did Lokesh feel when Zubin went quiet?
qa.a: Lokesh felt hurt and at first feared Zubin had stopped caring.

qa.q: What did Lokesh do that could bring Zubin back?
qa.a: Lokesh named the hurt gently and told Zubin exactly how to help, a meme on Tuesdays and a cricket visit on Saturday.
Zubin probably felt uncomfortable and helpless, not knowing what to say, as at the grandfather's funeral Zubin couldn't face.

grounding: The letter shows someone whose friend disappeared after a diagnosis out of discomfort, naming the hurt and telling the friend simple ways to help.

passage:
"You want to know who stayed? I'm Hemant, and honestly, the list surprised me.

When I got sick last year, three of my closest college friends vanished. Parveen, my best friend since school, didn't call for six weeks. I was hurt. I lay awake thinking, so that's what I meant to them.

Then Parveen's sister told me something. Parveen had been crying every time she picked up the phone, and then putting it down. She didn't know what to say.

So I called her. I said, 'You don't have to say anything right. Just come and eat samosas and tell me office gossip.'

She came the next day, with samosas and a lot of guilty tears. After that, every Thursday.

The other two I still hear from sometimes. That's okay. People are clumsy with illness. But I tell anyone who's sick now: tell your friends what you need. And hold on tight to the ones who show up."

qa.q: How long did Parveen go without calling?
How did Hemant feel when Parveen didn't call?
qa.a: Hemant felt hurt and wondered at night what Hemant had really meant to those friends.

qa.q: What turned things around with Parveen?
qa.a: Hemant called Parveen and said exactly what would help: no perfect words, just samosas and office gossip.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling during those six weeks?
qa.a: Parveen felt upset and helpless, crying each time she picked up the phone because she didn't know what to say.

grounding: The spoken account shows someone whose friends disappear during illness out of discomfort, telling a friend how to help and cherishing those who stay.
